title: A Little Princess
author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
short_summary: Wealthy young Sara Crewe is enrolled at Miss Minchin's strict London boarding school, where her imagination and kindness make her a favorite among the other students. When Sara's father dies and his fortune seems lost, Miss Minchin forces Sara into servitude as a scullery maid, cold and half-starved, yet Sara clings to the idea of being a princess in spirit no matter how she is treated. A mysterious, kind neighbor secretly helps her, and Sara's fortune and place in the world are eventually restored.
extended_summary:
Sara Crewe arrives at Miss Minchin's boarding school in London as a wealthy little girl with a vivid imagination, a generous heart, and a beloved doll named Emily. She quickly becomes a favorite of both students and teachers for her kindness, storytelling, and the elaborate birthday party her father arranges for her. But everything changes when news arrives that Sara's father has died and, it seems, lost his entire fortune in a risky investment. Miss Minchin, who once flattered Sara for her wealth, coldly strips her of her privileges and forces her to live in a bare attic room and work as an unpaid servant, given barely enough food and warmth to survive.

Through it all, Sara holds onto the idea that a true princess is defined not by money or comfort but by how she treats others, and she continues to be kind to the school's other servant girl, Becky, and to imagine comfort even in her cold, empty attic. Unknown to Sara, a mysterious and unwell gentleman named Mr. Carrisford has moved in next door, and it is gradually revealed that he was her father's business partner, believed his investment scheme actually succeeded, and has been searching for Sara ever since to give her back her rightful fortune. His servant secretly leaves Sara food, warm clothes, and comforts in her attic room before the full truth comes out and Sara's fortune, and her place in the world, are restored.

questions.prompt: On Sara's first morning at the school, Miss Minchin announces that Sara will begin French lessons. What does Monsieur Dufarge find when he speaks to her?

options: Sara already speaks French like a French child
Sara knows only a few words she learned from a book
Sara can read French but cannot say a word of it
Sara refuses to answer him in any language

questions.explanation: Sara's mother was French and Sara has spoken it all her life. She tries to explain this, but Miss Minchin will not listen — and is then shown up in front of the whole class. It is the first sign that Miss Minchin cares about how things look far more than about the child in front of her.

questions.prompt: Sara finds a coin in the mud on a freezing day and spends it at the baker's shop. How many of the buns does she keep for herself?

options: One of the six
Three of the six
All six of them
None of them

questions.explanation: Sara pays for four buns and the baker throws in two more 'for makeweight', so she has six. She has eaten almost nothing for days, yet she puts five of them into the lap of a beggar girl on the step and keeps one. This is the moment where being a princess inside costs Sara something real.

questions.prompt: While Miss Minchin says harsh things to her, Sara holds on to one rule about how she must behave: "A princess must be ___."
questions.explanation: Sara answers Miss Minchin quietly and correctly, however unfair the scolding is. The rule is not about manners for their own sake: as long as she keeps it, the cruelty around her cannot turn her cruel.

questions.prompt: Who is Melchisedec, the friend Sara makes during her first lonely days in the attic?

options: A rat who lives inside the attic wall
A sparrow that lands on the skylight
A stray cat that sleeps under her bed
A boy who works at the baker's shop

questions.explanation: Melchisedec is a rat living in the attic wall with a wife and a large family of his own. Sara saves crumbs for him out of her own small suppers and talks to him as a guest — she offers courtesy even to a rat, which is exactly what her idea of a princess means.

questions.prompt: Put these moments from Sara's years at the school in the order they happen.

items: Monsieur Dufarge tells Miss Minchin that Sara is already French
Sara is given the Last Doll at her eleventh birthday party
Sara's things are taken away and she is moved up to the attic
A little boy in the street presses his sixpence into her hand
Sara gives five of her six buns to a beggar girl
Sara wakes to find a fire lit and hot food in her attic

questions.explanation: Sara's fall happens in the middle of the story, not at the start: two happy years pass before the birthday party where the news of her father arrives. Everything that makes the book famous — the rat, the sixpence, the buns, the magic — happens afterwards, in the attic.

questions.prompt: Match each person to what they do in Sara's story.

right: The pupil who cannot learn her lessons and shares her books
The four-year-old who is told "I will be your mamma"
The servant who crosses the roof while the attic sleeps
The shop woman who puts two extra in the bag for nothing

questions.explanation: Sara is not saved by one rescuer. A slow classmate, a howling four-year-old, a servant from India and a baker who cannot even spare much all give her something — and each of them is treated by Sara as worth her full attention.

questions.prompt: Sort each moment by when it happens in Sara's life at the school.

content.groupA: While Sara is still the school's show pupil
content.groupB: After Sara is sent up to the attic

options.label: Monsieur Dufarge praises Sara's French accent
Sara promises Lottie that she will be her mamma
Sara is given the Last Doll and a party
Melchisedec takes crumbs from Sara's hand
Sara shares her buns with a girl in the rain
Sara's cold room is filled with food and blankets

questions.explanation: The line between the two halves is one afternoon: the birthday party. Sara's circumstances change completely at that point, but her behaviour — to Lottie, to Becky, to a rat, to a beggar — does not change at all. That steadiness is the whole argument of the book.

questions.prompt: When Miss Minchin scolds her, Sara silently thinks that she is a princess who could order Miss Minchin's execution but chooses to spare her. Why does the book say this pretending is good for her?

options: It stops her becoming rude and spiteful in return
It makes Miss Minchin nervous about punishing her
It helps her believe she will be rich again soon
It lets her stop noticing that she is cold

questions.explanation: The book is clear that while the thought held her, she could not be made rude and malicious by the rudeness and malice around her. Sara's pretending is not escape from her life — it is how she keeps command of her own behaviour inside it.

questions.prompt: Sara had eaten almost nothing for days when she gave away five of her six buns. Was that the right thing to do, or should she have kept more for herself? Give your reasons.
questions.explanation: Both positions can earn full marks. The strong 'yes' answer notices that the other child was starving worse than Sara and that giving is what makes Sara's princess idea real rather than a daydream. The strong 'no' answer notices that Sara was a starving child herself, that nobody was coming to feed her, and that she is not required to sacrifice her own health. Accept any answer that weighs Sara's own hunger against the other girl's.

questions.prompt: One night Sara falls asleep in a bare, freezing attic and wakes to find it changed: a fire burning, warm blankets, hot food on a little table. Imagine you could leave one gift there for her. What would you leave, and how would it help her get through the next day?
questions.explanation: There is no single right answer. A strong answer names one specific thing and says what it would do for Sara — keep her warm, feed her, let her go on telling stories, or something she could share with Becky next door. Sharing is worth noticing but is not required; any gift explained with a reason that fits Sara's life in the attic earns full marks.

questions.prompt: A little boy from the family next door stops Sara in the street and pushes his sixpence into her hand. What does Sara understand at that moment?

options: That she now looks poor enough to be a beggar
That the family next door has been looking for her
That Miss Minchin has been talking about her outside
That she is too proud to accept anybody's help

questions.explanation: She takes the coin rather than hurt his feelings — to be that proud, she decides, would be cruel — and afterwards wears it on a ribbon round her neck. But until that moment she had not known she might be mistaken for a beggar, and it stings more than hunger does.

questions.prompt: Sara invents names for the people she watches from her attic window. Because there are eight children in it, she calls the family next door the ___ Family.
questions.explanation: Sara names the world around her — the Large Family, Melchisedec, the Magic — because naming things is how she keeps them company. She gives each of the eight children a romantic invented name too, long before any of them speak to her.
